FWIW, here's my $.02. I agree with @tghosth here. I really don't think these deserialization-related requirements should be moved anymore than any of the other ASVS requirements in Chapter 5 should be moved. If you look at section v10.4, those are on "_general_ principles" supporting defensive coding, not specific techniques. If we move  V5.5 to v10.4, then we might as well move then entire Chapter 5 there because certainly input validation is a general defense and I think if anything fits under "defensive coding", that does. However, the techniques for deserialization defense are specific in nature. I know, as I've written a few in my day.

There are (at least) 2 distinct basic use cases that come into play here:
1. Verifying that serialized input came from a _trusted_ (based on the outcome of your threat model) source, implying that if you can confirm that the serialized input has a) not been tampered with and b) it actually originated from a trusted source (both of which you can do via cryptographic means like digital signatures, HMACs, or AEAD encryption) that you can use the serialized data "as-is" with otherwise validating the serialized data (although, I would contend it still is generally a good idea to do so, but that's something to decide in your threat model).
2. Verifying that serialized data that comes from a non-trusted source requires verifying that the data is "safe to use". What makes this tricky is that it may have to be verified in special ways because you can't deserialize it and check afterwards (does Chris Frohoff's [ysoserialize](https://github.com/frohoff/ysoserial) ring a bell?). In Java, you can white-list classes know to be "safe" (which is much trickier than it looks; I would not attempt it without some threat modeling) using something like [JEP 290](https://openjdk.org/jeps/290).

So, I don't think that these defensive techniques used to defend against deserialization vulnerabilities are general enough to move them to any code review section on defensive coding.

Therefore, I vote to close this issue. Or, if you really wish to continue to discuss it, I'd propose promoting it to a Discussion.

I gave examples with requirements 5.5.2 and 5.5.4, but I _assume_ I got arguments against those with requirements 5.5.3. If this is the case we don't talk about the same thing and there is no chance to find agreement.

So, instead of describing abstract deserialization, I go requirement by requirement. Otherwise, there is a risk of taking one detail or requirement out of context and applying it to all requirements.


**5.5.2**

> Verify that the application correctly restricts XML parsers to only use the most restrictive configuration possible and to ensure that unsafe features such as resolving external entities are disabled to prevent XML eXternal Entity (XXE) attacks.

It's about configuration or setup for library. Nothing about processing user input. Fits to V10 or to some configuration hardening. Also fits to "general principle" category.

The requirement may need an exception "if not intended by the application for controlled input" or something.

Like pointed out previously - the input validation part for processing XML is covered by other requirement:

> V13.3.1 Verify that XSD schema validation takes place to ensure a properly formed XML document, followed by validation of each input field before any processing of that data takes place.


**5.5.3**

> Verify that deserialization is not used when communicating with untrusted clients. If this is not possible, ensure that deserialization is performed safely, for example, by only allowing a allow-list of object types or not allowing the client to define the object type to deserialize to, in order to prevent deserialization attacks.

This requirement needs some work, the construction "Don't use it! But if you do, do it that way." does not make sense as a requirement.

This requirement describes handling safely untrusted input when (un)serializing, and fits to V5. I _assume_ this is also the requirement Kevin talked about and focused on.


**5.5.4**

> Verify that when parsing JSON in browsers or JavaScript-based backends, JSON.parse is used to parse the JSON document. Do not use eval() to parse JSON.

With or without untrusted input, eval() should never be used instead of JSON.parse(). It fits to V10.4. Also fits to "general principle" category.


**5.5.5**

> Verify that different parsers used in the application for the same data type (e.g. JSON parsers, XML parsers, URL parsers), perform parsing in a consistent way and use the same character encoding mechanism to avoid issues such as JSON Interoperability vulnerabilities or different URI or file parsing behavior being exploited in Remote File Inclusion (RFI) or Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.

It is about architecture or choice of components to be used in the application. I don't think it belongs to V5. Not sure it belongs to V10.4 either. But fits to "general principle" category.


Comments to @kwwall  https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1903#issuecomment-2015860600


> So, I don't think that these defensive techniques used to defend against deserialization vulnerabilities are general enough to move them to any code review section on defensive coding.

The conclusion from my text above is that there is a disagreement in 3 of 4 related requirements.


> Therefore, I vote to close this issue. Or, if you really wish to continue to discuss it, I'd propose promoting it to a Discussion.

FYI: for ASVS, we use issues to discuss certain categories or requirement-related problems or proposals, Discussions are used for more generic concepts. I'll close it when there is a decision and solution.
